questions.q: What does the shebang line #!/bin/bash do at the top of a script?
options: Adds a comment that bash ignores completely
Deletes the file after it finishes running
Tells the system which program (bash) should interpret and run the rest of the file
Automatically makes the file executable
questions.explain: The shebang tells the system which interpreter to use; without it, there's no reliable way to know the file should run as a bash script.

questions.q: Given SERVICE="nginx" earlier in a script, how do you read that value back?
options: $SERVICE
#SERVICE
@SERVICE
SERVICE
questions.explain: A leading $ tells bash to substitute the variable's stored value instead of treating the name as literal text.

questions.q: What keyword closes an if block in bash, and what closes a for loop?
options: Neither needs a closing keyword
fi closes a for loop; done closes an if block
fi closes an if block; done closes a for loop
end closes both an if block and a for loop
questions.explain: if blocks end with fi ("if" spelled backward); for loops end with done.

questions.q: A script with a valid shebang and correct commands still won't run as ./script.sh. What's missing, and what command fixes it?
options: It needs to be moved into /etc/systemd/system/
Nothing is missing — this scenario can't actually happen
The script needs to be renamed to end in .bash instead of .sh
The execute permission is missing; chmod +x script.sh adds it
questions.explain: Linux requires a file to have the execute permission before it can be run directly; chmod +x grants that permission.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say scripting matters for cloud automation specifically?
options: The same pattern — shebang, variables, conditionals, loops — is the building block for VM startup scripts, scheduled health checks, and multi-server deployment steps
Automation tools never use shell scripts, only graphical interfaces
Shell scripts cannot run on cloud virtual machines at all
Cloud providers require all scripts to be written in a special cloud-only language
questions.explain: Cloud VM startup scripts, scheduled checks, and deployment steps all build on exactly this pattern of shebang, variables, conditionals, and loops.
